questions.q: Which of the following is one of the six sections a capstone proposal needs, per this lesson?
options: Risks and fallback plan
A signed statement from a PhD advisor
A guarantee that the hypothesis will be confirmed
A full literature review of every paper in the subfield
questions.explain: The six sections are research question, hypothesis, method summary, related work, deliverables, and risks and fallback plan -- not a full literature review, an advisor's signature, or any guarantee of a confirmed hypothesis.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say writing the proposal before coding matters?
options: Because proposals are required by journals before any experiment can be run
Because it eliminates the need for a final written report later
It forces decisions about what's measured, what it's compared against, and what 'done' looks like while they're still cheap to change
Because code cannot technically be written without a proposal document existing first
questions.explain: The lesson states these three decisions are cheap to change on paper and expensive to change after code is written -- projects without a written proposal tend to drift in scope.

questions.q: In the worked proposal's hypothesis, what specific prediction is made about the 3-vs-5-qubit comparison?
options: The 5-qubit circuit will show a larger improvement because it has more qubits
The improvement from zero-noise extrapolation will be smaller at 5 qubits than at 3 qubits, because larger circuits accumulate more gate-error noise
The improvement will be identical at both qubit counts
Zero-noise extrapolation will have no effect at either qubit count
questions.explain: The worked hypothesis specifically predicts a smaller improvement at 5 qubits than 3 qubits, with the stated reasoning that larger circuits accumulate more gate-error noise for the same mitigation technique to correct.

questions.q: What does the worked proposal's 'risks and fallback plan' section name as a specific risk and a specific fallback?
options: The risk that Python might not be installed, with a fallback of switching languages
No specific risk is named anywhere in the worked example
IBM Quantum open-tier queue-time limits, with a fallback of reducing shots to 512 per factor and disclosing it in limitations
The risk that the paper might be retracted, with no fallback given
questions.explain: The worked example names queue-time constraints as a specific risk and reducing shot count (with explicit disclosure in the final report) as the specific fallback -- exactly the concreteness the lesson's self-review checklist asks for.

questions.q: Per the self-review checklist, what is wrong with a deliverables section that just says 'I will investigate X'?
options: Nothing is wrong with this phrasing
It should instead describe the hypothesis, not the deliverables
It is too specific and needs to be made vaguer
It isn't specific -- deliverables should name a specific figure, table, or report rather than a vague investigation
questions.explain: The lesson's checklist explicitly flags this: deliverables should name a specific figure/table or report, not a vague 'I will investigate X' phrasing.
